title: The P/E Ratio and What It Hides

cards.headline: A price tag on its own tells you nothing.
cards.body: One company's shares cost $12. Another's cost $400. Neither number tells you which business is expensive. Price only means something once you set it against what the company actually earns. That is the whole job of the P/E ratio.

cards.headline: It is one division, nothing more.
cards.body: Northwind Foods trades at **$60** a share. Over the last year it earned **$3** of profit per share. Sixty divided by three is **20**. Northwind has a P/E of 20: you pay $20 for every $1 of annual profit.

cards.headline: Read it as years of earnings.
cards.body: A P/E of 20 means you are handing over 20 years of Northwind's current profit to own one share today. That is the honest reading. It also shows why the number is only a starting question: earnings rarely stay still.
A trailing P/E divides by the earnings a company has already reported. A forward P/E divides by an analyst's [[1]] of next year's earnings — a number nobody has earned yet.
cards.explanation: Both get called the P/E. One is history, the other is a forecast dressed as arithmetic. Always check which one you are looking at.

cards.prompt: Two companies in the same industry. One trades at 9 times earnings, the other at 30. Which is the better buy?

options.label: You cannot tell from the P/E alone

cards.explanation: The gap is not a mispricing waiting to be collected. It is the market's forecast: the company at 30 is expected to **grow**, the one at 9 is expected to **shrink**. A P/E prices expectations, not quality.

cards.title: One retailer priced at half its peers
cards.caption: Four retailers, one industry, same year. Harborline is priced at half the multiple of every peer. That gap is not a bargain nobody noticed — it is a forecast that its earnings are falling.

cards.headline: The value trap, in one line.
cards.body: Harborline trades at $27 on $3 of earnings per share — a P/E of 9. Now suppose earnings fall to $1.50, as the market expects. That same $27 price is 18 times earnings. Cheap became expensive and the price never moved.
The ratio only works when the E can be trusted. In these three cases the number on your screen is arithmetic, not information.

stickers.label: A peak year for a cyclical

cards.summary: The P/E tells you what the market expects from a business, not whether that business is cheap.
bullets: P/E is price divided by earnings per share.
Trailing P/E is fact. Forward P/E is an estimate.
A low P/E often prices in shrinking earnings.
Compare a P/E to the company's own history or its rivals.

cards.insight: A P/E is not a price tag. It is the market's forecast written as a number — and forecasts can be wrong in both directions.
